title: Open files: find the entry square (part 3 of 3)
outcomes: Reads a position and names the open file and the half-open files, and the pawn trade that created each
Names the entry square before moving a rook onto an open file, and checks which pieces attack it
Knows a pawn can never guard a seventh-rank square, and a piece can: checks for the piece, not the pawn
Says what a defender can do (cover the entry square, contest the file, take it first) and finds the move that contests
Counts attackers and defenders on a pawn that blocks the file, and tells a protected blocker from an unprotected one
Explains the idea to a beginner with an example they can set up on a board

steps.text: Part 3 of 3: Open files: find the entry square. This part covers A real game; Teach it back. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**A real game.** Magnus Carlsen against Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, Tata Steel 2021, round 13. The c-file opened early by a pawn trade, and the game shows our three stages: take the file, face a contest, find the entry. The moves are facts from a broadcast database; the explanations are ours and labelled where they are guesses.

steps.prompt: In the game Vachier-Lagrave moved his rook off the c-file (...Rce8) to chase a pawn. [H] I think the c-file was already hard to hold. Do you think leaving it was a mistake, or the best of bad options? Write a reason, not just a verdict. The engine's opinion is a number; your reason is what you will use next game.

steps.caption: Back to the Carlsen game, a few moves on. After the c-file opens, Black offers a queen trade. Follow it and ask what changes.

line.say: Black takes on d4 with the c-pawn.
White recaptures with the c-pawn; the c-file is open.
The black queen offers a trade on d6.
White takes the queen.
The pawn recaptures. Queens are off, and the e-file is now half-open for Black.

claims.statement: After the queen trade the c-file is open, the b-file is half-open for White and the e-file for Black.

steps.caption: White to move. The c-file is open. Watch the rook take it, and what Black does about it.

line.say: The rook takes the open c-file at once. From c1 it attacks the bishop on c8 along the file.
Black develops the bishop to b7.
White develops the bishop to d3, which frees the first rank for the rooks.

claims.statement: The c-file is open, the b-file is half-open for White and the e-file for Black.
From c1 the rook attacks the bishop on c8.

steps.caption: Black to move, the same game. The white rook holds the c-file. How does Black answer it, and why does White step the king aside?

line.say: The knight comes to c6.
The king steps to d2, off the first rank. The rooks on c1 and h1 now see each other, so each backs up the other [I].
Black puts a rook on c8, opposite White's. A white rook landing on c7 would now be met by that rook [I]: the contest we saw earlier.

claims.statement: The c-file is open, the b-file is half-open for White and the e-file for Black.
After the king step the two white rooks are connected.

steps.caption: Black has left the c-file (the rook went to e8 to attack the pawn on e4). White to move. No black piece watches c7, but is landing there best? The engine prefers a3 first, to drive the knight away. An open entry square is a condition, not an order.

line.say: The pawn attacks the knight on b4. The engine rates this above the landing on c7 (depth 16).
The knight retreats to c6.
The bishop retreats to a2.
Black's rook takes the pawn on e4. White has given a pawn; the next board shows what it gets back.

claims.statement: No black piece attacks c7 in this position.
The pawn move a3 is the engine's first choice (depth 16).

steps.caption: Black's rook stands on e4 and the knight on c6 blocks its own bishop. White to move. Follow the exchange that ends with no black piece attacking c7.

line.say: The bishop attacks the rook on e4 from d5.
The knight steps to a5, so the bishop on b7 now attacks the bishop on d5.
White's bishop takes the rook on e4.
Black's bishop recaptures. White has won a rook for a bishop, and no black piece attacks c7 now.

claims.statement: After the knight move, the bishop on b7 attacks the bishop on d5.
At the end of the line no black piece attacks c7.

steps.caption: White to move. The same position as the question you just answered, now with the game continuation.

line.say: The rook lands on c7. No black piece attacks the square, and it attacks the pawns on a7 and f7.
Black moves the a-pawn to a6.

claims.statement: Rc7 is the engine's first choice (depth 16).
From c7 the rook attacks the pawn on a7.

steps.caption: The rook stays on c7. White now starts the h-pawn forward on the other wing, and Black has to answer on both wings. White to move.

line.say: White starts the h-pawn forward.
Black pushes the b-pawn to b5.
The h-pawn reaches h6 and attacks the bishop on g7.
The bishop retreats to f6.

claims.statement: The white rook still stands on c7.
The pawn on h6 attacks the bishop on g7.

steps.caption: Back to the first position. Check the entry squares. Now that you know what to look for, does the open e-file give a rook an easy landing?

claims.statement: Two black pieces attack e7: the bishop and the queen.
The engine counts h3 and Re1 among its first choices (depth 16).

steps.text: **The answer: not yet a landing.** The bishop and queen watch e7, and the queen, knight and rook watch e8, so a rook that jumped in would be taken. White may still put a rook on e1 to contest the file and tie pieces down; the engine counts that among its better moves (depth 16). The file here is a road to be fought for, not a landing.

**What to remember.** An open file is a road, not a prize. Find the entry square and count who watches it. Pawns never guard a seventh-rank square. Reach the file first, or contest it. A blocking pawn is protected or unprotected: treat them differently. A rook on an open file with no entry still ties pieces down. [H] Keep a list of the files you used in your own games and the squares you landed on; the pattern will teach you more than this page.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. Write four sentences for a beginner who knows how the pieces move: (1) what an open file is and what the entry square is, (2) when a rook on it works, (3) an example they could set up on a board, (4) one warning. Self-check: did you say what makes a file open, name the entry square, say when the landing fails, give an example a beginner could set up, and name one answer the defender has? Then look at your first guess and ask it again: was the e-file ready to use?

steps.text: **A model answer, to read after you wrote yours.** An open file has no pawn of either colour. The entry square is where a rook can land in the enemy camp, often on the seventh rank. It works when you arrive first, nothing covers the square, and something is waiting there. Example: a rook on d1, an empty d-file, no black piece watching d7. Warning: a bishop or knight covering the entry square can win your rook. A defender can cover the square or contest the file [I].

steps.prompt: Compare the model answer with yours. What did it include that you left out, and what did you say that it did not?

steps.text: **Remember.** An open file is a road, not a prize. Ask which square your rook can land on in the enemy camp, and count who watches it. If a piece guards that square, the rook can be taken, so contest the file instead of jumping in.
